Hi Miller.

Up until now, I hadn't seen how this card could be hated so much. But then,
it was because we would never had thought of doing something so drastically
unbalancing as "lending" or giving all your minions to someone for a kill,
or that kind of shit. Having seen it used on every final table and in every
optimized deck this week-end, and a few other times, I now stand among the
disgusted people. And Succubus on top of my hate list ? Dunno, lost another
9-Cap to PTO yesterday (GRRRRRRR !!!!!), but... At least, not everyone can
play PTO ; not everyone has to put it in his deck, if only for the contest,
or find a way to steal it. So, yes, Succubus as it now stands is
game-breaking and should not be allowed in tournaments.

> If it's not possible, then why shouldn't it be errated?

Why is it not possible that it be banned ?

> Proposals from our forum so far:
> - change it in an action at 1 stealth instead of master: location

Breaks it, but still makes it possible at the crucial time ; but it avoids
the "...and then you give it back to me" part. Still, it isn't the same
card. Might as well ban it. Not to mention that a Club is a Location, not an
action.

> - change it in a one-shot master card, ie not put into play,

All for it. Still potentially game-breaking, though, especially in the hands
of bad players.

and/or once
> a game a la Giant's Blood
> - stealable as a D action
> - burnable as a D action
> - usable only if the controler has got the edge
>
> any thoughts?

Once a game : see above.

Steal it could make things even worse, especially in presence of a weenie
deck (Palla, weenie Aus, Cel guns etc...).

Burn it doesn't change a thing in recursive (Anthelios !) decks. Remove from
the game is better.

The edge ? Madness Network anyone ?

I prefer removing it.

Anyway : something HAS to be done.

I've always seen the Succubus Club as just another thing that a good
deck / strategy has to plan for.

For example, it's well known that a possible reaction to an aggressive
combat predator is to stop transferring out minions (and it's
contestable whether this is "playing to win"). A decent combat deck
will plan for this, either by including bleed modifiers or being
suitably subtle and giving their prey the illusion that they have a
chance (and hence transfer out too many minions).

Same thing with Succubus Club. Don't let a player with the Succubus
Club get into a position where they think they could be a ding-dong
with it and or construct your deck to minimise the effect of such
behaviour.

Anyway, Succubus Club is quite vulnerable (being contestable,
arsonable, suddenable, subject to disputed territory etc). Not that
this is a particularly good argument for keeping it as is.

> And some abuses of the card can't even

> be stopped by virtue of "playing to win"...

What abuses of SC can't be prevented by enforcing a combination of
"play to win" and "no collusion"?

Do you mean a player in a "lost position" transfering their resources
for spite? It's pretty much axiomatic that a "lost position" entails
no significant resources.

Um, I don't see how self-ousting "gets (him) out of this losing position".
I suppose it IS spiteful towards ones prey and/or predator but I've never
understood that. Your predator and prey are supposed to be attacking you.
I've run into a few guys who seemed to think there was some necessity to,
for instance, "get back" at one's predator for being so successful at
preying on them but I think most people realize that's silly. Just as easy
to blame one's cross-table ally(ies) for not helping enough or putting
enough
pressure on the neighboring players. I've also seen this happen from time
to time and it usually looks pretty silly and spiteful, too.

If these people in Europe are just saying that the Succubus Club is bad
because it facilitates more effective spite plays, I suppose that's true.
But I'm more inclined to question the need for spite plays than to look at
banning Succubus Club. This may be one instance where it really IS
appropriate
to consider social ostracism (well, perhaps a mild form) to discourage what
is defined as lousy in-game behavior.

Fred

I have a Malk / FoS deck which uses 2 copies of Succubus Club. At
first I ran one SC, and a bunch of Malkavian Time Auctions, but I
traded for a second SC, cos it suits the deck better. The concept is
to play Form of Corruption, then give it away to my predator's
predator, to reduce the number of bleeds I take.

In this deck, I also use SC for minor trades and favours - like buying
a Blood Doll so I can put them on Hesha, or offering to rescue other
player's vampires for a pool. I once got my cross-table buddy to give
me a torpored vamp cos it was costing him pool (via Path of Lilith, or
something), and I didn't want the effect to oust him.

I feel that my use of SC is fine, and is entirely in the spirit of the
game.

...but the errata you suggest would hose the main purpose of SC in
this deck, and most of the minor uses too, so I don't like your
proposal.

Limiting the *size* of the trade rather than the type seems like it
would stop the abuse that is being bemoaned, and still allow the card
to be useful in kooky decks like mine.

For example:

+++
Succubus Club
Master: Unique location

During your untap phase, you may tap this card to trade with a
Methuselah who agrees to trade. Each Methuselah may trade up to 3
cards from their hand, 3 pool, and 1 card they control. The trade
cannot result in either Methuselah have fewer cards in hand than his
or her hand size. Any additional terms can be established, but none
are enforced by the rules.
+++

PS - I also like succubus club in combat decks. I think deals like
"give me your hunting ground, and I'll rush Arika for you" are quite
viable, and are not bad for the game.

Saying "well, someone has a Succubs Club in play. I had better not do
something perfectly reasonable that might make him act irrationally and
arbitrarily destroy the balance of the game..." is not a defense of the
card. It is a scathing indictment.

> I mean amongst the people I play with. My playgroup, my metagame or
> whatever term the cool kids are using for it these days.

Yeah, see, what happens in your group is mostly irrelevant to this
discussion. Maybe everyone in your group is perfectly rational and never
does anything stupid. Maybe no one in your group has ever realized that they
could do something spiteful and stupid. Maybe y'all are just lucky. Who
knows? The experiences of a single play group aren't really relevant in and
of themselves. The possibilites that the card allows for are.

> No, of course not. However, if someone proposes a deal in which you
> don't lose then you are no longer in a losing position. SC allows this
> to happen. The fact that you have the SC means that you are not in a
> losing position, assuming someone is willing and able to offer a deal.

Which is an argument that could go on for days and days, and drive the most
sane judge unsane. Your argument is "since you have the SC, you can never be
in a lost position". That isn't going to fly, nor is it going to convince
someone to not make a random, spiteful, game destroying move 'cause they
think they are in a lost position.

> a) this means you have to pander to the SC holder to a certain extent,
> so that they don't feel like this. Just like if someone else has most
> of the votes at the table, you have to be nice to them if you want your
> own votes to pass.

Pandering to a voter does not, generally, mean that voter can completely
destroy the balance of the table if the pandering goes badly.

Any "normal" dealing in VTES only has very limited tangible effect--I give
you some vote support, I don't attack your guy, I lend you some intercept
from my KRCG, I don't bleed you this turn, whatever. Succubus Club, on the
other hand, gives someone the power to completely circumvent a good portion
of the limits on the game (i.e. your ability to give things to people), as
well as giving them the ability to completely throw the balance of the game
out the window by virtue of a spiteful, one sided deal. Which is the problem
with the card.

All the rational discussion of how the card *can* be used for reasonable
purposes, and can be dealt with through reasonable actions do not nullify
the fact that the card can be, and often is, used for completely irrational
acts that tend to destroy a given game. That usually are the result of
spite. That the card *can* be used for such "deals" completely nullifies any
of the reasonable effects that the card can have in the long run.

> b) if their position really is lost then the swing due to their
> self-ousting "deal" will be small.

I give my predator 5 pool, 4 vampires, and a hunting ground. Your new
predator now has 11 more pool, twice the vampires he had just a turn ago,
and a new, free, hunting ground. This is a small swing?

> c) if their position isn't actually lost then they can't self-oust,
> which means it is a judging issue and/or an issue of sensible players.

If I can't reasonably oust my prey any time soon? I can make an argument
that my position is a lost one. It is unlikely that there will be any
argument gaainst such a claim that can be made that can't be counter argued
to the contrary. Meaning that the judge's life becomes a private hell. How
is this good for *a* game, let alone *the* game?

[Peter]

> Succubus Club, on the other hand, gives someone the power

> game (i.e. your ability to give things to people), as well as
> giving them the ability to completely throw the balance of the

Further to this, I can see your point that SC allows a player an
unusally large amount of freedom to be a dickhead. However, all these
"irrational" uses of the the card are already covered by the
anti-collusion, "play to win" and "unsportsman like behaviour"
provisions of the tournament rules.

Compare SC to the two banned cards "Madness of the Bard" and "Return to
Innocence".

"Madness of Bard" is banned, I believe, because it relies too much on
out of game issues like mastery of whatever language is being used by
the table.

"Return to Innocence" is banned because it results in large,
unpredictable pool swings (I believe). True, SC can also result in
large pool swings, but the crucial difference is that the large pool
swings from SC occur when it is being used in spite based, (probably)
illegal "deals"- i.e. already prevented by "play to win" etc. There
are plenty of other game advancing uses for SC. By comparison, "Return
to Innocence" only has one use (large pool swings) and is perfectly
legal from a "play to win" perspective.

The "bad uses" of SC are already prevented by the rules. It's just a
matter of enforcing them. If you happen to play in an environment
where the rules aren't enforced, that's your problem. If that's the
case, you're playing just as different and irrelevant a game from me as
those playing in a "havok" environment.

lehrbuch wrote:

> Maybe. I'm not quite trying to say that though. I'm saying that to
> ignore the fact that your predator has a SC is stupid. The fact that
> they have a SC changes what is reasonable (to a certain extent).

Sure. But that they have a Succubus Clud gives them a *rediculous* ability
to affect the game that is unprecidented in relation to any other card. If,
like, my predator is a vote deck, and can play Parity Shift, I have to take
that into account when I generate extra pool. That is a reasonable
modification of behavior based on what your opponents are playing. Having to
modify your behavior to prevent your opponent from completely destroying the
game, simply because he is playing the one card that really lets him do that
is just silly.

> Any experience you've had is equally irrelevant. What's your point?

That I'm not talking about how *I* deal with Succubus Club in *my*
playgroup. I am discussing what SC can be used to do. And sometimes is. And
that is why it is wholly inappropriate for competetive play.

> Of course, I see the "generally" in your statement. Equally SC is not
> "generally" used in an effective, legal, spiteful stab at another
> player.

No. But it can be. And that it can be is a problem. That it isn't *usually*
used for these purposes do not balance out that sometimes it is.

Return to Innocence wasn't *always* used to bleed someone unblockably for
15. Sometimes it was used to bleed someone for 6 at zero stealth. That
sometimes the latter happened didn't mean that the former was ok. So Return
to Innocence was banned from play. Cause it was a completely inappropriate
card.

I fully realize that usually, SC is used to, like, say, extort someone for a
few pool, or trade vampires or something. But occasionally it is also used
to completely ruin games out of spite. Because it can be. If the card had
safeguards built into it that prevented this sort of thing, then it would
likely be just fine. Or if it had some disincentive to play (like a built in
burn clause), it would be less likely to see play, and consequently, less of
an issue. But as it stands, even if it is *usually* used for completely
valid reasons, sometimes it isn't. And those times *completely* make the
card inappropriate for competetive play.

> It's a player problem. Not a card problem.
>
> Players can equally easily screw up the game by standing up and
> leaving. Or by picking up their library and searching for the hand
> they want. Or by deciding to start with 40 pool.

Yeah, see, most of those are very easy to control, cut and dry, cheating.
You can't search through your deck for the hand you want. 'Cause it is
cheating. You can't decide to start with 40 pool. 'Cause it is cheating. You
can get up and leave, but the result of that is much smaller than getting up
to leave *and* giving all of your pool and vampires and cards to another
player.

See, the examples you give are *easily* avoided. Someone declaring that they
are in a "lost" position and then using that as a justification to hose the
whole table via a one sided suicide SC "deal" is not easily avoided.

And then, to boot, there are no cards in the game that specifically give you
an in game mechanism to get up and leave the table, search through your deck
for the hand you want, or starting with 40 pool without a specific reason.

Succubus Club, however, *specifically* gives you the mechanism to, should
you feel warranted to do so, get up to leave *and* give all of your pool and
vampires and cards to another player.

It is a good idea to make rules that prevent people from searching their
deck for the hand they want and to prevent people from starting with 40
pool. It is also a good idea to provide disincentive to get up and leave a
game for no good reason (usually results in a DQ). Why isn't a good idea to
remove from the game a specific mechanism that allows for incredibly
disruptive behavior, that is *way* too difficult to make illegal?

> And completely nothing to do with the game. This is still a problem of
> players not cards.

Succubus Club *gives you the mechanism* to do this in game. No other card
does that. Yeah, you can play stupid, or spiteful, or just leave a game. But
these have built in disincentive to them, and only very limited tangible
effects. SC allows you to completely circumvent a main limiting factor of
the game (i.e. you can't randomly give stuff to people) and in doing so, it
also allows you to completely screw up a game if you want to. I realize that
this is as a much a problem with players as it is with the card in question,
but I have no control over how my opponents play--if they want to be
spiteful or stupid, I can't really stop them. But I can suggest that a card
that makes spite or stupiditiy a very concrete and game affecting motive be
removed as it is just bad for the game.

> This was a lost position?

Sure. I have 5 pool and 4 vampires and a hunting ground. My prey has 15
pool, 5 vampires, a lot of intercept, and aggro damage. I don't have much,
if any, stealth. I'm not getting through my prey ever.

The concept of trying to keep the Succubus Club in check by arbitrating what
is or is not a "lost" position is absurd, as someone is always going to be
able to make a viable argument as to how they are in a "lost" position.

I'd much rather be playing a game where whether or not someone is in a "lst"
position was irrelevant. With SC in play, someone's position being "lost" or
not can be a *huge* issue. Without SC? Who cares? What difference does it
make?

> Not if you can hang around for the 1/2 VP for making it to the time
> limit.

Yeah, see, I'm unwilling for the game to hinge on such an argument one way
or the other. These "I'm in a lost position" vs. "no you aren't and here is
why..." arguments are absurd. Especially when a game is actually going on.

Remove the Succubus Club, and you remove the primary *need* to even have
such an argument.

That such arguments even exist is a problem.

> Which is why player arguments are irrelvant to a judge's decision
> (ideally).

Again, overtaxing an already overtaxed judge.

The whole saftey valve that keeps Succubus Club from being abused or cheated
with is "judge discression". It strikes me as a patently bad idea to have a
single card that is only kept in check by judges discression.

If the Succubus Club had significant limits on what it could or could not
do? It'd probably be fine--maybe if it allowed you to trade up to 2 pool in
exchange for a single card in play. Or something like that. But without
completely re-writing the card, this isn't going to happen. And I don't
think the card is getting completely re-written. So removing it from play
strikes me as a much better plan than leaving it there.

Six events that can be burned by a single card that requires Black Hand.

Versus six master cards that can be burned with a +1 stealth inherent vote.

Sure, six ARs currently in play may be devastating. That's six pool each
turn regardless of anything else. However, having the rougher events in
play may be equally devastating. Consider the following Gehenna cards:

1. Wormwood. five counters. Maximum vampire capacity is 5.
2. Veil of Darkness
3. Blood Weakens
4. Fall of the Sabbat
5. Fall of the Camarilla
6. Recalled to the Founder - Note that maximum capacity is 5.

Now imagine a deck with small bleeding vampires (not any more cornercase
than an Anson deck). Or an Anarch Barons voter deck. Or a weenie Trap -
Undead Persistance for deck. The sum of these six cards is that:

- All vampires are independent and sect-based cards are basically unusable.
- When you play your first discipline-requiring card, it may fizzle (note
that if it was an action modifier or reaction, it still counts as having
been played).
- You do not replace discipline-requiring cards until the end of the
action.
- Every vampire is capacity 5 or less. Excess blood drained off long ago.
- You burn a vampire each untap if you control 2 or more of the same clan.
Since all vampires are capacity 5 or less, you never become immune to this
effect.

different cards, sure, but Entrancement is incredibly limited, requires

On the subject of which is nastier, it's arguable as to which is more
game-changing.

Someone gaining 6 pool (and a VP) can be hugely game changing, yes.
However, someone gaining two torporised vampires, a Hunting Ground, a
copy of Oxford University, and your remaining 2 pool *and* 6 pool and a
VP as you oust yourself and give them what you have could also be game
changing.

Which is bigger? That depends on the game. For a weenie deck, an extra
vampire or two might not be much against the 7 they have. For a Fatima
Multi-Rush support deck, an extra couple might be really useful. For a
deck with only one vampire itself, a couple more possibilities might be
really good.

However, you're also confusing KRC with Succubus Club in other ways too.

Succubus Club is a unique, free, master location. You can either
contest it or burn it or cancel the master card. (Bear in mind that one
of the old 'definitions' of "broken" is turning the game into X or anti-
X. This isn't quite the same, of course, but it seems sensible to think
about it.)

KRC can be stopped with intercept, which can stop any action
(potentially). KRC can be stopped with vote cancellation, which can
affect a huge portion of the game. KRC can be stopped by doing things
like rushing vampires (a common strategy) before they can call it, or
other vampire "manipulation" (also common strategies). KRC can be
stopped by vote defence - titles, vote gaining and so on.

One problem with Succubus Club is that it does allow you to do a *lot*
with vastly reduced possibilities for interaction, relative to its
power.

Is that enough to think it broken? I don't know.

I think you're missing something crucial here. A judge needs to be
there for *everything* every player says or does, to see if it rhymes.
And the judge needs to know a *lot* about things which are ordinarily
nothing to do with the game. Do a search on what issues have been
brought up on the group before. Brief ones that spring to mind are
questions about words rhyming with themselves, whether you have to rhyme
internally to a sentence or across sentences, whether it would need to
have any rhythm to it (since it may not be rhyming sentences if you just
happen to rhyme on the end word after an arbitrary length of words -
certainly, that seems to violate designer intent), eye rhymes (visual
rhyming), Irish rhymes (a perfectly legitimate rhyming scheme), how much
you are allowed to mutilate the pronunciation of a word - bear in mind
that in Pope's time, say, "tea" and "obey" were perfectly reasonable
rhymes[0]. Can I go for that pronunciation in order to rhyme? Then,
depending on which of these are allowed or not, consider the
difficulties in a multitude of languages where they may or may not have
sufficient scope to do such things, and where 'rules' on rhyming may be
very, very different. Additionally (for extra credit), consider if it's
desirable that a player with, for example, an extremely wide but obscure
vocabulary could be rhyming perfectly legitimately under all the above
rules - but unfortunately, no-one else on the table can understand a
word he or she says. Can you do anything about that? Madness of the
Bard specifically wants players to do rhyming sentences, and it seems
unfair to require the player to say it again in some other format where
he may or may not be able to come under the rhyming scheme you dictate
in the rules.

However, in brief, collusion is defined in the Guidelines. As has been
gone over before, if you don't think it's verifiable Collusion, there
are other rule-based avenues to deal with undesirable attempts to
subvert the rule structure or disrupt a tournament. Things like proper
behaviour are *always* judgement calls.

A "losing deal", IMO, is one where a player is throwing away a chance at
a game win for some other reward (typically, a VP or two). A "winning
deal" is not really relevant, since a judge does not have to think about
these in detail - and one might regard some deals as not being losing
but possibly not being the best deal they could get. But that's not
something the judge has to intervene over, since no player is (or can
be) forced to make, offer or take certain deals. This requires a
relatively laissez-faire but objective judgement of the table. You may
care to discuss this with the player, so that they can talk to you about
what they're trying to. This, then, isn't based on just the judge's
intuition since they can determine a lot from other sources too.
Certainly, a judge should not (IMO) be aggressively interventionist and
have to deal with dotting every i and crossing every t in a deal else
you end up preventing the players from playing the game and making their
own mistakes - they just make yours, instead.

IMO, a player playing to win is the default assumption. It's only when
a player starts acting out petty real-life arguments (Unsportsmanlike
Conduct), taking losing deals and so on that you have to really start
worrying. Again, someone may not be taking the best options towards
winning - but that doesn't mean the judge intervenes. Essentially, I
almost never look at it from "Is this player trying to win?" but rather
"Is the player trying to throw the game away, for whatever reason?"

Rather, I'd point to just the three I see played far more often in "event"
decks (since the others suck) - Blood Weakens, The Slow Withering, Veil of
Darkness.

I'm sure the obvious elements to playing with these in play don't need to be
recounted. I will note that I fail to see why the Lasombra and, to a lesser
extent, the Kiasyd needed a hoser that might actually see play. It's
interesting that these help weenie decks. Something I realized about The Slow
Withering is that it encourages people to play Dominate. Can't get more bang
for your buck at inferior than Conditioning and Deflection. The alternative to
Deflection, Telepathic Misdirection, becomes much less delightful at double the
cost (when it works at all).

>True. Time will tell how useful Gehenna cards will become for actually
>winning.

New sets will change the environment. How about deciding now that Gehenna
events have much too much random effect on games?

Why? Because you don't control what your opponents play. When I saw Recalled
to the Founder hit play for the first time, it became obvious that this was by
far the most important weakness of events. Sure, you could decide to not play
an event because it's more likely to hurt the wrong player(s), but then, you
built your deck a certain way for an environment that doesn't exist.

Alternatively, if you buy into the idea that you can control what your
opponents play by the very existence of events, they will either build decks
that aren't as screwed by them or some decks that were previously viable cease
to be. That last isn't all bad as CCGs should evolve and, as one thing becomes
weaker, something else should become stronger, but because there's no guarantee
that events will see play the possibilities of events seeing play and not
seeing play lead to a more random or narrow play environment. This is much
like why so many people hate AR decks. Decks that are viable with no AR deck
at the table can be entirely screwed if there is one. The opposite is also the
case. If you can't be too sure of whether you expect to see an AR deck, you
play only those decks that function whether one is played or not, greatly
limiting the field.

Most Gehenna events are essentially hosers. Anthelios not so much. Hosers can
help you win, otherwise no hoser would ever see play. They can also hurt one's
chances for winning by being dead draws or being weaker than other draws. And,
their global nature, requirements, and costs means that a lot of decks have to
build toward them to take advantage of them. The deck that has the greatest
advantage at a table with an event deck isn't likely to be the event deck but
the deck that could have played the events and decided to spend those slots on
better cards.

Not sure the focus of this post was that great. I just haven't ranted much
about events in forums.

You're mis-reading what I'm saying.

What I'm saying - on one hand - is that comparing the spite of a cross-
table KRC to the spite of Succubus Club is apples and oranges.

Votes have multiple defences which are very commonly used by decks and
are multi-functional defence. Similarly spiteful, but basic, plays are
similarly countered in many basic, necessary defences. If I decide to
spitefully through a Fame at you and rush you, so you die before I do,
you can Obedience the rush, or defend in the combat, or block with
another vampire, or D.I. the rush, or hit me back harder, or tap The
Elysium, or throw in Illusions of the Kindred, or have some weapons/guns
which will let me go to long range, or have a Secure Haven, or...
Similarly, votes have all the usual counters - block, cancel, vote down,
pro-actively remove your votes, etc.

All of these things can be very easily re-used if they don't come up
against that specific play. Generic defences have a very wide-range of
utility against a wide range of plays. It doesn't matter if that
specific spiteful play doesn't come up.

If, on the other hand, you play Sudden Reversal, Bleeding the Vine or
location destruction. Sudden Reversal and Bleeding the Vine must both
be in hand (or out) prior to Sudden Reversal being played which is a
relatively high opportunity cost compared to the swing it can make. If
you don't have Vox Domini/Delaying Tactics in hand or Vox Senis out when
the KRC comes out, the worst that can happen is 3 pool. Similarly, you
can play Arson - but location destruction rarely makes up a large
portion of a deck.

On the other hand, there may be reasons why a specific metagame doesn't
need to account for spiteful uses of Succubus Club. For a start, it's
not (as Peter has explained, at length) a case of people actively using
Succubus Club to win.

This isn't, say, a case of Return to Innocence being used and you MUST
USE IT OR DEFEND AGAINST IT OR YOU DIE. The problem being discussed is
that of spiteful use. Since spiteful use, in the "I'm lost, here, take
my stuff" sense, is entirely a choice and not a sensible necessary
decision in response to an escalation of power levels, some groups
simply won't encounter it and have no need to encounter it. It's not
like the RtoI experience (or Tomb or whatever) where playing it is
better than not playing it. Similarly, it may be a particularly poor
player who uses such "tactics" where the difference isn't that huge.
Again, there's no need for it to be good players using it.

Not encountering it because it's not a no-brain good play doesn't mean,
well, anything really.

On the other other hand, if a single card (or very small group of cards
using similar effects e.g. a bunch of Corruption cards) requires groups
to shift into particular defences against it, there may be a problem.
This is not proof positive, but it is sufficient to raise eyebrows.
